vignette:
Rohan traces the start of it all back to a business trip eight months ago. He was in a taxi, navigating a city where the language was a melody he couldn't decipher, when the blare of a siren cut through the traffic noise. The car was forced to the curb by men in mismatched uniforms. The world dissolved into a chaos of shouting he couldn't understand, the incomprehensible chatter pressing in on him as he was pulled from the car. The days that followed are a blur of a windowless room and a disorienting, sickening dizziness. His captors would bind him to a chair and spin him until the world became a nauseating vortex, a state of helpless vertigo where he couldn't tell up from down. It was a torture of the senses, of control, and it ended as abruptly as it began, with him being left on a roadside, his passport in his pocket.

Now, at fifty-eight, Rohan finds that the room has followed him home. His work as a product manager, once a source of pride, has become a landscape of threats. During a team meeting, when several colleagues speak at once, the overlapping voices cease to be English and instead become that same terrifying, incomprehensible wall of sound. A familiar wave of dizziness washes over him, his vision tunnelling. He has to excuse himself, hand pressed to the wall for balance, his heart hammering against his ribs. He has since come to believe that any situation with the potential for stress is a risk he cannot take. He delegates high-stakes presentations and avoids the chaotic but crucial brainstorming sessions, a move his team perceives as aloofness. He is certain there is something fundamentally wrong with him, a weakness they must all see. He feels that if he had been stronger, smarter, or less conspicuous on that trip, none of this would have happened.

His home, once a sanctuary, offers little relief. He lives in a state of constant, humming vigilance, unable to truly relax even in his favourite armchair. His wife, Meera, has learned not to approach him from behind. A simple, affectionate touch on his shoulder can make him recoil with a choked gasp, his body reacting before his mind can register her presence. He feels a deep, gnawing shame each time it happens. He is convinced that people, even those who love him, cannot be truly trusted; their actions are unpredictable and could bring harm at any moment. At night, sleep is shallow and fleeting. He wakes several times, his body rigid, straining to hear any unfamiliar sound. He'll get up and walk the perimeter of the house, checking the locks on the doors and windows, his mind cataloguing escape routes.

He has built a fortress of avoidance around himself. He has mapped out new routes to work to avoid driving past the local police station, the sight of a uniform enough to make his palms sweat. He constantly monitors his own body, a sentry on guard for the first hint of lightheadedness, certain it signals an impending collapse. He interprets every headache, every moment of fatigue, as a sign that his body is failing him, that the damage is permanent. He sees his future as a flat, grey expanse. When his manager recently mentioned a potential promotion, Rohan felt a surge of panic, not pride. He was sure that nothing good could happen to him anymore, that any opportunity was simply a precursor to a new, more devastating failure. It was after Meera found him one night, standing silently in the dark living room at 3 a.m., that she told him she couldn't watch him disappear anymore. He has come to therapy not out of hope, but out of a quiet desperation, terrified of losing the last footholds of the life he once knew.
